screens.title: Dictionaries: key-value maps in Python
screens.narratorSegment: Dictionaries are one of Python's most useful collection types because they let you associate meaningful identifiers with values. Think of a dictionary like a phone book: you look up a person's number by their name, not by a numeric position. In this lesson you will understand what makes a dictionary different from lists or tuples, how keys must be immutable and unique, and why values can be any type. We'll practice creating dictionaries, reading and writing entries, and using safe access patterns that avoid runtime errors. You will see common utility methods such as keys, values and items, and learn removal operations like del, pop and popitem. I will also show practical scenarios — a simple inventory and a contact book — so you can see dictionaries used to model real data. By the end you'll know typical pitfalls, such as KeyError when a key is missing, and how get or membership checks avoid those errors. Keep an eye out for the example cards: they show concrete code you can run immediately. Why does this matter? Dictionaries give you fast lookup by name or ID, making them ideal for configuration, lookups, and small databases inside a program. As you proceed, ask yourself: what unique identifier would I use for the data I need to model?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: A dictionary maps unique, immutable keys to values. Use it when you need named access rather than numeric indexing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Dictionaries Overview

Dictionaries in Python

Named lookup, mutable storage, keys must be unique and immutable.

Definition

A dictionary is a collection of key-value pairs enclosed in curly braces. Lookups use keys instead of numeric indexes.

Why it matters

Fast access by identifier makes dictionaries ideal for configuration, small caches, and modeling structured records like user profiles.

Example — literal creation
# Creating simple dictionaries
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30, "city": "New York"}
student_grades = {"Math": 95, "Science": 88, "History": 92}
empty_dict = {}
Key Takeaway

Use dictionaries when you need to associate unique keys with values and perform frequent lookups or updates by key.

Coming up

Access patterns, safe reads, mutation, and practical inventory/contact examples.

Visual Concept
Keys (immutable, unique)
Strings, numbers, tuples
Values (any type)
Numbers, lists, nested dicts
Quick Topics
Access, add/update, remove, iterate, methods, KeyError avoidance
Explore Key Topics
Access & get() — safe reads
Mutation — add, change, delete
Iteration & view objects

screens.title: What you'll be able to do
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map directly to practical skills you will develop while learning Python dictionaries. First, you'll be able to define what a dictionary is and describe its key properties — unordered and mutable — and explain the immutability requirement for keys with examples. Second, you'll create dictionaries and access values safely, using both direct indexing and the get method, and you'll know when to prefer one over the other. Third, you'll add, update, and remove entries using assignment, del, pop and popitem while understanding the error behavior and return values. Finally, you'll iterate efficiently over keys, values, and items and recognize when a view object is dynamic and how to convert views to lists. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual to help you remember the pattern, and a verified competency milestone that suggests a practical check: run a small script that builds and edits a contact book without errors. These steps together give you both conceptual understanding and practical fluency with dictionaries.

screens.title: What is a dictionary?
screens.narratorSegment: A dictionary is a collection of key-value pairs where each unique key maps to a value. Keys must be immutable and unique; that means strings, numbers and tuples can be keys, while lists or other mutable containers cannot. Values are unrestricted — they can be numbers, strings, lists, other dictionaries or even functions. Dictionaries are mutable, so you can change, add or remove entries after creation. In older descriptions dictionaries were described as unordered, meaning their iteration order was not guaranteed; in modern Python insertion order is preserved in common implementations, but you should not rely on ordering for algorithms that require strict sorted or stable order unless you explicitly sort keys or use an OrderedDict. A common misconception is to treat dictionaries like lists with numeric indexes: unlike lists, dictionary access uses keys rather than positional indexes, and you won't reach for integer counters unless those integers are meaningful keys. A concrete example is mapping a username to a profile object. Understanding the immutability requirement is practical: trying to use a list as a key will raise a TypeError because the list is not hashable. Takeaway: think about what uniquely identifies each value; that becomes your dictionary key. How would you model a product catalog where each product has a fixed SKU? Use the SKU as the dictionary key.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Dictionary = key-value pairs. Keys must be unique and hashable; values can be any type. Use for named access.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › What is a dictionary?
Definition

A mapping from unique, immutable keys to values. Mutable collection and fast for lookups by key.

Key rules
  • Keys must be hashable: strings, numbers, tuples allowed.
  • Values accept any type and can be duplicated.
  • Mutable: you can add, change, or delete entries.
Common misconception

Do not treat dictionaries as ordered lists. Even though insertion order is preserved in recent Python versions, avoid relying on it for logic that requires explicit ordering.

Key Takeaway

Pick keys that uniquely and immutably identify values. That design choice makes lookups simple and fast.

Concrete example
# Map usernames to profiles
profiles = {
  "alice": {"age": 30, "city": "NY"},
  "bob": {"age": 25, "city": "SF"}
}
# Tuple key example (allowed)
coords_map = { (10, 20): "landmark" }
Why this matters

Choosing an appropriate key transforms many problems into constant-time lookups. For example, use user IDs or SKUs rather than searching through lists for a match.

Misuse example

Attempting to use a list as a key raises a TypeError because lists are not hashable. Use tuples instead if you need a compound immutable key.

screens.title: Create and access dictionaries
screens.narratorSegment: Creating dictionaries is straightforward: use curly braces with key-colon-value pairs, or start empty with a pair of braces. Accessing values by key uses square bracket notation; for example, using the print function to show person name accesses person["name"]. That direct access is concise but will raise a KeyError if the key does not exist. The get method is a safer alternative: it returns None or a specified default when a key is missing. A typical pattern is to use get when keys may be optional or when you want a fallback default. A common beginner mistake is to use direct indexing everywhere and then encounter KeyError in production data where some keys are absent. Another pattern is to test membership with the in operator before indexing. Both patterns are valid; choose get when you need a default and membership when missing keys indicate a logic error you want to catch. Concrete code helps: the shown examples create person and student_grades dictionaries, then demonstrate direct prints and get calls with and without a default. Takeaway: prefer get(default) in flexible reads and direct indexing when you expect a key to be present and want errors surfaced quickly.

keyIdea.title: Access patterns
keyIdea.text: Use direct indexing for required keys; use get(default) or membership checks to avoid KeyError for optional keys.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Create & Access
Code examples
# Creating dictionaries
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30, "city": "New York"}
student_grades = {"Math": 95, "Science": 88, "History": 92}
empty_dict = {}

# Direct access (can raise KeyError)
print(person["name"])            # Alice

# Safe access with get
print(person.get("city"))       # New York
print(person.get("country"))    # None
print(person.get("country", "Unknown"))  # Unknown
Example scenario

When reading configuration values that may be missing, get with a default avoids crashes and provides sensible fallbacks.

Patterns
  • Direct indexing when a missing key is a programming error.
  • get(default) for optional keys or user-supplied data.
  • Membership check with in operator when you want explicit branching.
Common mistake

Relying exclusively on direct indexing with unpredictable input leads to KeyError. Use get or membership checks instead.

Check your understanding

If get returns None, how would you distinguish between an explicit stored None value and a missing key? Consider using a unique default marker or checking membership first.

screens.title: Add and modify entries
screens.narratorSegment: Modifying dictionaries is simple: assign a value to a key to add or update an entry. If the key is new, assignment creates it; if the key exists, assignment replaces the value. This twin behavior means you can use the same syntax for both adding and updating. When updating nested structures, be cautious: modifying a mutable value in place will change the stored object for all references. The lesson example uses person["occupation"] = "Software Engineer" to add a new field and person["age"] = 31 to update an existing one. A common pitfall is accidentally overwriting complex values; for example, assigning a new list to a key replaces the previous list unless you explicitly extend it. Another useful technique is setdefault, which returns the value for a key and sets it to a default if missing — handy for grouping or building nested dictionaries without repeated membership checks. Concrete scenario: in an inventory, decrementing a stock count involves reading the current value, subtracting the sold quantity, and writing the result back. Always think about whether you want to mutate the value in place or replace it entirely. Closing question: when would you prefer setdefault or defaultdict patterns over simple assignment?

keyIdea.title: Mutation
keyIdea.text: Assign to add or update keys. Be careful with in-place mutation of stored mutable values and consider setdefault for grouped initialization.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Add & Modify
Code walkthrough
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}
# Add a key
person["occupation"] = "Software Engineer"
# Update a key
person["age"] = 31

# Use setdefault to initialize a list for grouping
groups = {}
groups.setdefault("admins", []).append("alice")
Example scenario

In inventory code, substract sold quantities and write back the updated count to the same key to keep stock accurate.

Common pitfall

If a value is a list and you modify it in place, any other reference to that list sees the change. Decide whether to copy or replace depending on intent.

Key Takeaway

Assignment both adds and updates. Use setdefault for safe initialization and be intentional about in-place mutation.

Pro tip

For nested counters consider collections.defaultdict(int) in larger programs, but setdefault is handy in small scripts.

screens.title: Removing entries: del, pop, popitem, clear
screens.narratorSegment: Python provides several ways to remove entries from a dictionary, each with slightly different semantics that are useful in different situations. The del statement deletes the specified key and its value but raises a KeyError if the key is missing. pop removes the key and returns its value; if the key is missing you can provide a default to avoid an exception, otherwise a KeyError is raised. popitem removes and returns an arbitrary pair; its typical use is to consume items one at a time, for example when processing until empty. clear removes all items from the dictionary, leaving an empty mapping. Choose the method that matches your intent: use pop when you need the removed value, del when you want the exception as a signal for logic errors, and popitem when order doesn't matter and you want to process items iteratively. Be careful: relying on popitem's arbitrary removal is fine for algorithms that treat the dictionary as an unordered set, but if you need deterministic behavior, extract keys in sorted order before removing. A concrete example shows del person["city"] and student_grades. pop("Science") to demonstrate returned values and mutation. Closing thought: when removing items from a dictionary during iteration, iterate over a static list of keys to avoid runtime modification issues.

keyIdea.title: Removal methods
keyIdea.text: Use del for strict deletion, pop to remove and retrieve safely, popitem to consume items, and clear to empty a dictionary.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Removing entries
Code examples
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 31, "occupation": "Software Engineer"}
# del removes, raises KeyError if missing
del person["occupation"]

# pop returns a value, with optional default
grade = {"Math":95, "Science":88}
science_grade = grade.pop("Science")   # returns 88
missing = grade.pop("Art", None)      # returns None, no error

# popitem removes an arbitrary pair
pair = grade.popitem()

# clear empties the dictionary
person.clear()
Practical note

When deleting while iterating, iterate over a copy of the keys list to avoid modifying the dictionary during iteration.

When to use which
  • del: you expect key present and want an error if not.
  • pop: you want the removed value and safe default handling.
  • popitem: consume entries without concern for order.
  • clear: reset the dictionary.
Common mistake

Using del without checking can raise KeyError unexpectedly on user data. Use pop with a default for safer deletion when keys may be absent.

Check your understanding

Which method would you use when you need the removed value for logging? Which would you use if you want to signal an error when a key is absent?

screens.title: Dictionary view objects: keys(), values(), items()
screens.narratorSegment: Dictionaries offer view objects for inspecting content: keys(), values(), and items(). These return dynamic views that reflect changes to the dictionary after they are created. That means if you capture dict. keys() and then add or remove entries, the view updates to show the new content. Views are lightweight and efficient for many inspection tasks, but sometimes you need a stable snapshot; convert the view to a list to freeze the content at a point in time. Another important detail is that items() yields pairs as tuples, which is convenient for simultaneous key and value unpacking in loops. A common misunderstanding is assuming view objects are lists — they are not; they behave like set-like and mapping views and do not support list-specific methods, so converting to list is necessary for indexing or repeated stable access. Example code demonstrates list(person. keys()) and iterating with for key, value in person. items(): print formatted strings. Takeaway: use views for live inspection, convert to lists when you require a snapshot or indexed access. What snapshot would you take before mutating during iteration? Dictionary view objects: keys(), values(), items() means keys(), values(), items() return dynamic views. convert to list() for a stable snapshot when needed.. In practical terms, dynamic views and converting to lists for stable snapshots.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: View objects
keyIdea.text: keys(), values(), items() return dynamic views. Convert to list() for a stable snapshot when needed.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › View objects
Quick code
person = {"name":"Alice", "age":31, "city":"NY"}
keys_view = person.keys()
print(keys_view)             # dynamic view
person["country"] = "USA"
print(keys_view)             # reflects new key

# Snapshot
keys_list = list(person.keys())
print(keys_list)
When to snapshot

Snapshot before mutating while iterating, or when you need stable indexed access to keys or items.

Iteration pattern

Use for key, value unpacking: for key, value in person.items(): process both without extra lookups.

Common confusion

Don’t assume the view supports list methods or indexing. Convert to list when you need those behaviors.

Key Takeaway

View objects are efficient and live. Convert to list for a stable snapshot before mutating during iteration.

screens.title: Iterating dictionaries
screens.narratorSegment: Iterating through dictionaries can be done in several ways, each suited to a task. Direct iteration yields keys, which is handy when you only need the identifiers. Use dict. keys() to be explicit. Use dict. values() when you only care about values, and dict. items() when you need both key and value in the same loop. The items approach avoids repeated lookups and is often the most efficient when both pieces are needed. Another pattern is iterating over a snapshot of keys when you plan to mutate the dictionary inside the loop. A common misconception is that iterating items() yields copies — it yields tuples of references; modifying a mutable value inside the loop can affect the original stored object. Concrete examples show for key in person: print key and person[key]; for key, value in person. items(): formatted printing; for value in person. values(): aggregate computations like sum. Takeaway: choose the iteration method that matches the information you need and be cautious when mutating during iteration. Try converting items to a list if you must remove keys during the loop.

keyIdea.title: Iteration patterns
keyIdea.text: Use direct iteration for keys, values() for values only, and items() for both. Snapshot keys before mutating during iteration.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Iterating
Examples
person = {"name":"Alice","age":31,"city":"NY"}
# Keys
for key in person:
    print(f"Key: {key}, Value: {person[key]}")

# Items (preferred when you need both)
for key, value in person.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")

# Values
for value in person.values():
    print(value)
Performance note

items() avoids extra dictionary lookups when you need both key and value, which is often slightly more efficient and clearer.

Mutating while iterating

If you remove keys while iterating, iterate over list(dict.keys()) to work on a snapshot and avoid runtime errors or skipped items.

Key Takeaway

Match the loop to the data you need. Prefer items() when you need both key and value and snapshot keys before mutating.

Check

Which iteration would you choose to compute the sum of numeric values in a dictionary? Try values() and items() versions to compare.

screens.title: Practical example — inventory management
screens.narratorSegment: This practical inventory example ties together several dictionary operations you have learned. We model inventory as a dictionary where keys are product names and values are quantities. The script prints the current inventory, simulates a sale by checking membership and comparing quantities, updates quantities by assignment, adds a new item by assignment, and then checks for low-stock items by iterating through items. It also demonstrates using sum on inventory. values() to compute the total stock. Common mistakes include assuming a key exists and subtracting without checking, which can raise KeyError or lead to negative stock values. The example includes membership checks and an else branch that handles missing items. This small scenario demonstrates adding, modifying, accessing, and iterating in one cohesive example and shows how dictionaries model dynamic application state. Try modifying the code to return a message if a sale would result in negative stock — that's a natural extension and a useful validation step. Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Inventory Example
Inventory script
inventory = {
  "apples": 50,
  "bananas": 100,
  "oranges": 75,
  "grapes": 20
}

print("--- Current Inventory ---")
for item, quantity in inventory.items():
    print(f"{item.capitalize()}: {quantity}")

# Simulate a sale
item_sold = "apples"
quantity_sold = 10
if item_sold in inventory:
    if inventory[item_sold] >= quantity_sold:
        inventory[item_sold] -= quantity_sold
        print(f"
Sold {quantity_sold} {item_sold}.")
    else:
        print(f"
Not enough {item_sold} in stock. Only {inventory[item_sold]} available.")
else:
    print(f"
{item_sold} not found in inventory.")

# Add a new item
inventory["mangoes"] = 30

# Low stock check
for item, qty in inventory.items():
    if qty < 30:
        print(f"Warning: {item.capitalize()} stock is low ({qty})")

# Total items
total_items = sum(inventory.values())
print(f"
Total items in stock: {total_items}")
Lessons from the example
  • Check membership before subtraction to avoid KeyError or negative counts.
  • Use assignment to add new items and iteration to find low stock.
  • sum(inventory.values()) quickly aggregates numeric values.
Key Takeaway

Dictionaries model mutable state well. Validate values before mutating to maintain correct application state.

Try this

Modify the script to prevent negative stock by refusing the sale and logging a message.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Contact Book
Starter code
# 1. Create empty dictionary
contact_book = {}
print(f"Initial contact book: {contact_book}")

# 2. Add contacts
contact_book["Alice Smith"] = "123-456-7890"
contact_book["Bob Johnson"] = "987-654-3210"
contact_book["Charlie Brown"] = "555-123-4567"
print(f"After adding contacts: {contact_book}")

# 3. Update a contact
contact_book["Bob Johnson"] = "999-888-7777"
print(f"After updating Bob's number: {contact_book}")

# 4. Retrieve a contact
alice_number = contact_book["Alice Smith"]
print(f"Alice Smith's number: {alice_number}")

charlie_number = contact_book.get("Charlie Brown")
print(f"Charlie Brown's number (using get()): {charlie_number}")

# 5. Handle missing contact
david_number = contact_book.get("David Lee", "Contact not found")
print(f"David Lee's number: {david_number}")

# 6. Remove a contact
del contact_book["Charlie Brown"]
print(f"After removing Charlie Brown: {contact_book}")

# 7. List all contacts
print("
--- All Contacts ---")
for name, phone in contact_book.items():
    print(f"Name: {name}, Phone: {phone}")
Why this is useful

A contact book maps names to numbers directly, supporting constant-time lookup and simple update flows for real applications like address books.

Common error

Using del on a missing contact raises KeyError. Prefer get for reads and pop with a default for deletions when data is uncertain.

Allow multiple numbers by storing lists as values and use setdefault to initialize the list when adding a second number.

screens.title: Dictionaries vs lists, tuples and sets
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding when to use a dictionary instead of a list, tuple or set is important for clear design. Use a list when you need an ordered sequence of items accessible by position. Tuples are like immutable lists for fixed collections. Sets provide membership tests and uniqueness but do not associate keys to values. Dictionaries shine when you need to map identifiers to values, enabling constant-time lookup by name or ID. A common misunderstanding is trying to store records as lists of lists instead of using dictionaries keyed by an ID; this complicates lookups because you must scan the entire list. Another contrast is using a list of tuples for small lookups — that is valid but inefficient for frequent lookups. The contact book and inventory examples show situations where dictionaries provide simpler and faster code. If you need order plus mapping semantics, keep in mind that insertion order is preserved in modern Python, but explicit ordering should be handled with sorting when required. Takeaway: choose dictionaries for named access, lists for sequences, tuples for fixed records, and sets for unique collections and membership tests.

screens.title: Common errors and defensive patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Two common errors crop up when working with dictionaries: KeyError from accessing or deleting a missing key, and TypeError when attempting to use an unhashable key like a list. KeyError is a runtime signal that a key is absent; sometimes that's desirable because it surfaces bugs, and sometimes it's not, so use get with a default for optional access or membership checks when you want to branch. For deletions, prefer pop with a default to avoid exceptions when removing user-supplied keys. TypeError from unhashable keys happens when you attempt to use mutable objects as keys; the remedy is to use immutable equivalents such as tuples, or to convert complex keys into strings. Defensive patterns include validating input, using get(default) to supply graceful fallbacks, and converting view objects to lists before mutating. A concrete example: wrapping dictionary access in a try-except block can be appropriate when you must handle missing keys explicitly; otherwise prefer safer methods. Final thought: defensive design reduces runtime surprises and makes your code easier to reason about when the data you receive is uncertain. fullNarratorScript:
Dictionaries are one of Python's most useful collection types because they let you associate meaningful identifiers with values. Think of a dictionary like a phone book: you look up a person's number by their name, not by a numeric position. In this lesson you will understand what makes a dictionary different from lists or tuples, how keys must be immutable and unique, and why values can be any type. We'll practice creating dictionaries, reading and writing entries, and using safe access patterns that avoid runtime errors. You will see common utility methods such as keys, values and items, and learn removal operations like del, pop and popitem. I will also show practical scenarios — a simple inventory and a contact book — so you can see dictionaries used to model real data. By the end you'll know typical pitfalls, such as KeyError when a key is missing, and how get or membership checks avoid those errors. Keep an eye out for the example cards: they show concrete code you can run immediately. Why does this matter? Dictionaries give you fast lookup by name or ID, making them ideal for configuration, lookups, and small databases inside a program. As you proceed, ask yourself: what unique identifier would I use for the data I need to model?

These objectives map directly to practical skills you will develop while learning Python dictionaries. First, you'll be able to define what a dictionary is and describe its key properties — unordered and mutable — and explain the immutability requirement for keys with examples. Second, you'll create dictionaries and access values safely, using both direct indexing and the get method, and you'll know when to prefer one over the other. Third, you'll add, update, and remove entries using assignment, del, pop and popitem while understanding the error behavior and return values. Finally, you'll iterate efficiently over keys, values, and items and recognize when a view object is dynamic and how to convert views to lists. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual to help you remember the pattern, and a verified competency milestone that suggests a practical check: run a small script that builds and edits a contact book without errors. These steps together give you both conceptual understanding and practical fluency with dictionaries.

To make these objectives concrete, this screen lists small checks and a short micro-project you can run. For defining dictionaries, write three short examples using strings, integers and tuples as keys and explain why a list cannot be used as a key. For safe access, practice both direct indexing and get with a default; intentionally attempt a missing key and observe the difference between a KeyError and returning None. For mutation, perform an add, an update and a remove using assignment, pop, and del, and note the return values or exceptions. For iteration, write loops using keys(), values() and items(), and convert a view to a list to demonstrate that views are dynamic. The recommended micro-project is a contact book that uses a dictionary to map full names to phone numbers; include add, update, retrieve and delete flows and print the contents after each operation. These hands-on checks ensure you can reason about dictionary behavior as well as run working code.

A dictionary is a collection of key-value pairs where each unique key maps to a value. Keys must be immutable and unique; that means strings, numbers and tuples can be keys, while lists or other mutable containers cannot. Values are unrestricted — they can be numbers, strings, lists, other dictionaries or even functions. Dictionaries are mutable, so you can change, add or remove entries after creation. In older descriptions dictionaries were described as unordered, meaning their iteration order was not guaranteed; in modern Python insertion order is preserved in common implementations, but you should not rely on ordering for algorithms that require strict sorted or stable order unless you explicitly sort keys or use an OrderedDict. A common misconception is to treat dictionaries like lists with numeric indexes: unlike lists, dictionary access uses keys rather than positional indexes, and you won't reach for integer counters unless those integers are meaningful keys. A concrete example is mapping a username to a profile object. Understanding the immutability requirement is practical: trying to use a list as a key will raise a TypeError because the list is not hashable. Takeaway: think about what uniquely identifies each value; that becomes your dictionary key. How would you model a product catalog where each product has a fixed SKU? Use the SKU as the dictionary key.

Creating dictionaries is straightforward: use curly braces with key-colon-value pairs, or start empty with a pair of braces. Accessing values by key uses square bracket notation; for example, using the print function to show person name accesses person["name"]. That direct access is concise but will raise a KeyError if the key does not exist. The get method is a safer alternative: it returns None or a specified default when a key is missing. A typical pattern is to use get when keys may be optional or when you want a fallback default. A common beginner mistake is to use direct indexing everywhere and then encounter KeyError in production data where some keys are absent. Another pattern is to test membership with the in operator before indexing. Both patterns are valid; choose get when you need a default and membership when missing keys indicate a logic error you want to catch. Concrete code helps: the shown examples create person and student_grades dictionaries, then demonstrate direct prints and get calls with and without a default. Takeaway: prefer get(default) in flexible reads and direct indexing when you expect a key to be present and want errors surfaced quickly.

Modifying dictionaries is simple: assign a value to a key to add or update an entry. If the key is new, assignment creates it; if the key exists, assignment replaces the value. This twin behavior means you can use the same syntax for both adding and updating. When updating nested structures, be cautious: modifying a mutable value in place will change the stored object for all references. The lesson example uses person["occupation"] = "Software Engineer" to add a new field and person["age"] = 31 to update an existing one. A common pitfall is accidentally overwriting complex values; for example, assigning a new list to a key replaces the previous list unless you explicitly extend it. Another useful technique is setdefault, which returns the value for a key and sets it to a default if missing — handy for grouping or building nested dictionaries without repeated membership checks. Concrete scenario: in an inventory, decrementing a stock count involves reading the current value, subtracting the sold quantity, and writing the result back. Always think about whether you want to mutate the value in place or replace it entirely. Closing question: when would you prefer setdefault or defaultdict patterns over simple assignment?

Python provides several ways to remove entries from a dictionary, each with slightly different semantics that are useful in different situations. The del statement deletes the specified key and its value but raises a KeyError if the key is missing. pop removes the key and returns its value; if the key is missing you can provide a default to avoid an exception, otherwise a KeyError is raised. popitem removes and returns an arbitrary pair; its typical use is to consume items one at a time, for example when processing until empty. clear removes all items from the dictionary, leaving an empty mapping. Choose the method that matches your intent: use pop when you need the removed value, del when you want the exception as a signal for logic errors, and popitem when order doesn't matter and you want to process items iteratively. Be careful: relying on popitem's arbitrary removal is fine for algorithms that treat the dictionary as an unordered set, but if you need deterministic behavior, extract keys in sorted order before removing. A concrete example shows del person["city"] and student_grades. pop("Science") to demonstrate returned values and mutation. Closing thought: when removing items from a dictionary during iteration, iterate over a static list of keys to avoid runtime modification issues.

Dictionaries offer view objects for inspecting content: keys(), values(), and items(). These return dynamic views that reflect changes to the dictionary after they are created. That means if you capture dict. keys() and then add or remove entries, the view updates to show the new content. Views are lightweight and efficient for many inspection tasks, but sometimes you need a stable snapshot; convert the view to a list to freeze the content at a point in time. Another important detail is that items() yields pairs as tuples, which is convenient for simultaneous key and value unpacking in loops. A common misunderstanding is assuming view objects are lists — they are not; they behave like set-like and mapping views and do not support list-specific methods, so converting to list is necessary for indexing or repeated stable access. Example code demonstrates list(person. keys()) and iterating with for key, value in person. items(): print formatted strings. Takeaway: use views for live inspection, convert to lists when you require a snapshot or indexed access. What snapshot would you take before mutating during iteration? Dictionary view objects: keys(), values(), items() means keys(), values(), items() return dynamic views. convert to list() for a stable snapshot when needed.. In practical terms, dynamic views and converting to lists for stable snapshots.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Iterating through dictionaries can be done in several ways, each suited to a task. Direct iteration yields keys, which is handy when you only need the identifiers. Use dict. keys() to be explicit. Use dict. values() when you only care about values, and dict. items() when you need both key and value in the same loop. The items approach avoids repeated lookups and is often the most efficient when both pieces are needed. Another pattern is iterating over a snapshot of keys when you plan to mutate the dictionary inside the loop. A common misconception is that iterating items() yields copies — it yields tuples of references; modifying a mutable value inside the loop can affect the original stored object. Concrete examples show for key in person: print key and person[key]; for key, value in person. items(): formatted printing; for value in person. values(): aggregate computations like sum. Takeaway: choose the iteration method that matches the information you need and be cautious when mutating during iteration. Try converting items to a list if you must remove keys during the loop.

Tuples are like immutable lists for fixed collections. Sets provide membership tests and uniqueness but do not associate keys to values. Dictionaries shine when you need to map identifiers to values, enabling constant-time lookup by name or ID. A common misunderstanding is trying to store records as lists of lists instead of using dictionaries keyed by an ID; this complicates lookups because you must scan the entire list. Another contrast is using a list of tuples for small lookups — that is valid but inefficient for frequent lookups. The contact book and inventory examples show situations where dictionaries provide simpler and faster code. If you need order plus mapping semantics, keep in mind that insertion order is preserved in modern Python, but explicit ordering should be handled with sorting when required. Takeaway: choose dictionaries for named access, lists for sequences, tuples for fixed records, and sets for unique collections and membership tests.

Two common errors crop up when working with dictionaries: KeyError from accessing or deleting a missing key, and TypeError when attempting to use an unhashable key like a list. KeyError is a runtime signal that a key is absent; sometimes that's desirable because it surfaces bugs, and sometimes it's not, so use get with a default for optional access or membership checks when you want to branch. For deletions, prefer pop with a default to avoid exceptions when removing user-supplied keys. TypeError from unhashable keys happens when you attempt to use mutable objects as keys; the remedy is to use immutable equivalents such as tuples, or to convert complex keys into strings. Defensive patterns include validating input, using get(default) to supply graceful fallbacks, and converting view objects to lists before mutating. A concrete example: wrapping dictionary access in a try-except block can be appropriate when you must handle missing keys explicitly; otherwise prefer safer methods. Final thought: defensive design reduces runtime surprises and makes your code easier to reason about when the data you receive is uncertain.
